name: DevUtils
tagline: A native offline toolbox of small developer utilities: JSON formatting, JWT decoding, base64, timestamps, regex, hashes, and friends.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: DevUtils is a well made bundle of tiny, well understood transformations: parse this, decode that, format the other thing. Every single one of those tools is a pure function over a text box, with no server, no account, and no data anyone else owns. An agent can produce a local page with the fifteen or twenty tools you actually use in a single session, and it will be correct because the specs are all public and boring. What you are really buying from DevUtils is that someone already did it, made it native, and made it fast to reach. That is polish, not a moat, and polish is exactly the thing you get to trade away when the user is you.
coreLoopDIY: A single local web page with a searchable list of text-in, text-out developer tools that runs entirely in the browser with no network calls.
requirements: optional: keep it running as a pinned tab or wrap it in a tiny desktop shell later
whatYouLose: Native app feel: global hotkey, menu bar presence, instant launch, no browser tab hunting
Automatic clipboard detection that guesses which tool you wanted before you pick one
The long tail of tools you forgot existed until the day you needed one, like cron parsing or certificate decoding or line sorting
Someone else maintaining edge cases in the fiddly parsers and keeping up with new formats
Confidence that a sensitive token pasted into it never leaves the machine, which you now have to guarantee yourself by reading your own code
moatNotes: The trust angle is real but shallow: people paste secrets into it and want a signed offline native binary. A local build you wrote yourself satisfies that just as well, arguably better.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a paid, signed, offline native app is the cheapest way to stop thinking about a category of chore forever. Forty dollars once versus an evening of your life plus the low background hum of maintaining your own regex tester is a defensible trade, especially when the app is genuinely fast and the hotkey means you never break flow. The DIY version wins on cost and loses on the moment you need the one tool you did not build.
notes: One of the purest one-shot targets on this site: no state, no network, no other users, just pure functions with a nice front end.
prompt:
Build a local, offline-first developer utility toolbox as a single-page web app.

Stack, non negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. No backend, no database, no accounts, no analytics, no telemetry, no network requests at runtime. Everything runs client side. No .env file is needed because there are no secrets.

Layout: left sidebar with a searchable list of tools, main panel with the selected tool. Cmd+K opens a command palette that fuzzy-filters tools and switches to one on Enter. Remember the last used tool and the last input per tool in localStorage. Dark mode by default, light mode toggle.

Every tool follows the same shape: an input textarea, an output pane, a copy button, a clear button, and inline error text when parsing fails. No modals. No toasts that block anything.

Implement these tools:
1. JSON: format, minify, sort keys, and show a collapsible tree view.
2. JSON to YAML and YAML to JSON.
3. JWT decoder: header, payload, exp and iat rendered as human dates. Decode only, do not verify signatures, and say so in the UI.
4. Base64 encode/decode, with a toggle for URL-safe alphabet.
5. URL encode/decode plus a query string parser that renders params as a table.
6. Unix timestamp converter: seconds and milliseconds, local time and UTC, plus a live "now" button.
7. Hash generator: MD5 via a small library, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512 via WebCrypto.
8. UUID and ULID generator with a count field.
9. Regex tester: pattern, flags, highlighted matches over the test string, and a capture group table.
10. Text tools: case conversion, line sort, dedupe, trim, line count, character count.
11. HTML entity encode/decode.
12. Cron expression explainer: turn a five field expression into plain English plus the next five run times.
13. Diff: two panes, line level diff with additions and deletions colored.
14. Color converter: hex, rgb, hsl, with a swatch preview.

Out of scope: any native wrapper, any clipboard monitoring, image or file tools, anything that uploads bytes anywhere.

Write tests with Vitest for the pure transform functions, especially the timestamp, cron, and JWT parsing. Ship a README with one command to run it and one command to build a static bundle I can open from disk.
